_**Fighting Vipers**_[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-7) is a 1995 [fighting video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_game "Fighting game") developed by [Sega AM2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_AM2 "Sega AM2") and published by [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega") for [arcades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcade_video_game "Arcade video game"). A [3D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_computer_graphics "3D computer graphics") fighter, it uses the same game engine as AM2's _[Virtua Fighter 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtua_Fighter_2 "Virtua Fighter 2")_ (1994), but features enclosed arenas and an armor mechanic, and was targeted more towards Western audiences, using a U.S. setting and more freeform styles of martial arts.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag11-8)

The game was released in November 1995 in arcades, using the [Sega Model 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Model_2 "Sega Model 2") hardware, before it was [ported](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porting "Porting") to the [Sega Saturn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Saturn "Sega Saturn") home console in 1996. Though _Fighting Vipers_ was not very popular in North American arcades,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-EGM91-9) the Saturn version was one of the most high-profile games in the system's 1996 holiday lineup,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-10) and was met with positive reviews. A sequel was made, _[Fighting Vipers 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers_2 "Fighting Vipers 2")_ (1998), and all characters in the original also appeared in a crossover with _Virtua Fighter 2_, _[Fighters Megamix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighters_Megamix "Fighters Megamix")_ (1996).

_Fighting Vipers_ features a similar style of gameplay to Sega AM2's more renowned _[Virtua Fighter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtua_Fighter "Virtua Fighter")_ series, specifically _[Virtua Fighter 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtua_Fighter_2 "Virtua Fighter 2")_, using simply guard, punch and kick attack buttons with a focus on combo moves. The Saturn version uses its three extra buttons for three smaller combos.

Each of the 9 characters featured in the game wears armor that can be broken off by opponents, leaving them more vulnerable to taking damage.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-11) A human shaped meter in the top corners of the screen monitors damage to the armor. Walls surround each arena, caging the combatants in, allowing for attacks in conjunction with them (bouncing off etc.).[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-12) If a knockout attack is strong enough, characters can knock their opponent over, on top, or straight through the walls.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag11-8)

The Saturn port of _Fighting Vipers_ added Playback Mode and Training Mode, both of which are now used widely in the fighting genre. Players could save their matches and play them again in Playback Mode, while Training Mode talked the player through the moves of each character one-by-one.

Main Characters

*   **Bahn**:

Despite only being a 17-year-old high school student, Bahn is a powerful and imposing fighter in a long coat and hat. Hailing from Nishino Town, Japan and declared himself as Genghis Bahn III, he has come overseas to find and fight his father, whom he has never met and abandoned him and his mother when he was a boy.

Voiced by Sega designer Kazunori Oh in the first two main games, and [Hiroki Takahashi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroki_Takahashi "Hiroki Takahashi") in _Project X Zone_.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-Kazunori_Oh-13)

*   **[Candy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey_/(Fighting_Vipers/) "Honey (Fighting Vipers)")** (**Honey** in the Japanese version):

A petite 16-year-old fashion student with a pleasant nature, Candy designed her own trademark plastic fairy costume herself, and has entered the tournament to promote her original fashion line.

*   **Grace**:

A 19-year-old African-American born in Armstone City whose armor is themed after the protective gear for inline skating, including the skates themselves. Grace is making her living as a fashion model. Though she once dreamed of becoming a professional figure skater, her lover and coach betrayed her, leaving her disillusioned.

*   **Raxel**:

The [narcissistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narcissism "Narcissism") lead singer and guitarist for a hair metal band called 'Death Crunch' with [KISS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiss_/(band/) "Kiss (band)")\-styled armor and a red [Gibson Flying-V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibson_Flying-V "Gibson Flying-V") electric guitar, Raxel is the son of an Armstone City councilman, a drop out who left home after a fight with his father. Raxel has entered the tournament to heighten his own profile and become more famous.

*   **Tokio**:

A 16-year-old Japanese American pretty boy with a sense of justice rebelling against a strict kabuki actor's household. Tokio is a former leader of a street gang called 'Black Thunder' but left after feeling responsible for another gang member's death. He entered the tournament for a challenge and for thrills.

*   **Sanman**:

A mysterious fat man about whom nothing is known, other than his birthday (3 March) and an obsession with the number 3, hence his name (_san_ is Japanese for "three").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag11-8) Sanman drives a large customized scooter. Picky is the only person whom he befriends.

*   **Jane**:

A butch and muscled 18-years-old part-time construction worker, Jane trained her whole life to join the Navy, but did not make it past training. She was discharged after repeatedly losing control of herself during fights and injuring fellow seamen. Jane now wants to test just how tough she is, hence entering the Fighting Vipers tournament.

Voiced by Cara Jones.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-Cara_Jones-14)

*   **Picky**:

A young stereotypical skateboarder who attended Armstone campus, Picky's armor is styled after protective gear for skateboarders. He carries his skateboard on his back, and hits opponents with it. He is a 14-year-old middle schooler.

*   **Mahler**:

A mysterious 20-years-old masked wrestler, who wears a poisonous snake armor and holds a grudge against the Mayor of Armstone City (who has organised the tournament). He was not officially registered as a participant of the first Viper tournament. He is an unlockable character.

*   **B.M.**:

The main antagonist of the series, he is the mayor of Armstone City and in fact the organizer of the tournaments. B.M. is a powered-up version of Mahler.

Sega Saturn exclusive guest characters

*   **Kumachan**: a 10-year-old smiling bear character wearing an orange hat, who is included as an [unlockable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret_character_/(video_games/) "Secret character (video games)") character in the Sega Saturn port. It is based on the giant floating balloon mascot seen in the Old Armstone Town stage. It uses Sanman's fighting style, and its 2nd player counterpart is called Pandachan. Even though it can fight, its 3D model never moves.
*   **[Pepsiman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepsi#Pepsiman "Pepsi")**: the Japanese mascot of [Pepsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepsi "Pepsi") who only appears in the Japanese Sega Saturn version of the game as an unlockable character.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-15) He was removed from the US and PAL releases.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SSM27-16)

_Fighting Vipers_ was developed using the same game engine which was first used for _[Virtua Fighter 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtua_Fighter_2 "Virtua Fighter 2")_, and uses a nearly identical arcade board, though with slightly faster processing speed.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag2-17) Unlike _Virtua Fighter 2_, there are no ring-outs; producer [Yu Suzuki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yu_Suzuki "Yu Suzuki") stated, "We received comments about the ring-outs in _VF_ indicating different changes, \[_[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic "Sic")_\] and so for _FV_ the fighting can continue mercilessly."[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-18)

The character Mahler was created by reducing the power specifications of the boss, B.M., so that he would be appropriately balanced for player vs. player matches.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag13-19)

A demo of the game was displayed at the 1995 [JAMMA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JAMMA "JAMMA") show with all eight characters playable, though they did not yet have all their moves available.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag2-17)

The Saturn conversion, like the arcade original, was developed by Sega AM2.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-20) The programming team consisted of 15 people, most of whom had worked on the Saturn version of _Virtua Fighter 2_, and some of whom had worked on the arcade version of _Fighting Vipers_.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag13-19) Work on the conversion began in the first quarter of 1996[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-21) and took eight months. After converting the _Virtua Fighter 2_ engine, the team focused first on recreating the barriers, as they anticipated this would be the most difficult part to accomplish on the Saturn hardware.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag13-19) Because armor and walls can be broken in the game, there was no easy way of reducing the number of polygons in those elements.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag13-19) In part to compensate for the lower polygon counts on the characters, a new form of dynamic lighting incorporating [Gouraud shading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gouraud_shading "Gouraud shading") was added to the Saturn version.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag11-8) In order to make this effect possible, and have the game run at a speed comparable to the arcade version, the team decided at the beginning of development that they would not use the Saturn's high-resolution mode.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag13-19)

### Regional differences

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fighting_Vipers&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Regional differences")\]

The original Japanese version had a large amount of advertising for [Pepsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepsi "Pepsi"), due to [product placement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_placement "Product placement") agreements with Sega at the time. This licensing was removed in the US and PAL versions because the [promotional campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promotional_campaign "Promotional campaign") involving Pepsi was never taken outside of Japan.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SSM27-16)

In the Japanese version, the character Candy is named Honey.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SSM27-16)

In Japan, _Game Machine_ listed _Fighting Vipers_ on their December 15, 1995 issue as being the most popular arcade game at the time.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-31) It went on to be one of the top five highest-grossing arcade [printed circuit board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printed_circuit_board "Printed circuit board") (PCB) software [of 1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_in_video_games "1996 in video games") in Japan.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-32) It was considerably less popular in North American arcades.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-EGM91-9)

Reviewing the arcade version, _[Next Generation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Next_Generation_/(magazine/) "Next Generation (magazine)")_ called _Fighting Vipers_ "a beautiful, highly polished, polygon-rendered and texture-mapped game featuring brand new characters, unprecedented closed-in arenas (for a 3D fighter), a slightly different set of fighting strategies using armor, and a more cinematic style of viewing." The reviewer also praised the more intuitive button combinations used to execute moves. Despite this, he concluded that the game fails to measure up to recent fighting games, chiefly due to the "strained" character designs: "Raxel, Jane, Picky, Sanman are undeniably trendy and conclusively uncool ... They lack the artful, graceful movements of _[VF2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtua_Fighter_2 "Virtua Fighter 2")_'s Lau, Sarah, or Pai."[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-NGen12-27)

In reviews for the Saturn version, the barrier mechanics - allowing players to beat opponents against or through walls and use them to launch attacks - were met with universal approval.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-EGM88-25)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-GSrev-26)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-NGen24-28)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag12-29)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-GPro99-33) Most were also enthusiastic about being able to break off an opponent's armor for extra damage,[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-EGM88-25)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-GSrev-26)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-NGen24-28)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag12-29) though Crispin Boyer and Sushi-X of _[Electronic Gaming Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Gaming_Monthly "Electronic Gaming Monthly")_ felt the amount of flesh exposed when a fighter's armor is broken off amounted to cheap lewdness.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-EGM88-25) While some complained of reduced polygon counts and occasional slowdown compared to the arcade version,[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-GSrev-26)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-GPro99-33) the conversion to the Saturn as a whole was well-regarded, with critics especially praising its retention of the arcade version's smooth animation, its use of light sourcing, and the Saturn-exclusive features.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-GSrev-26)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-NGen24-28)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag12-29)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-GPro99-33) _[GameSpot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpot "GameSpot")_ concluded, "If you have a Saturn, this is the fighting game to own. If you don't, _Fighting Vipers_ gives you a good reason to get one."[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-GSrev-26) _[GamePro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GamePro "GamePro")_ said it "is one of our favorites because it's fast, sexy, and easy."[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-GPro99-33) And while most critics felt that _Fighting Vipers_ clearly falls short of _Virtua Fighter 2_,[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-EGM88-25)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-GSrev-26)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-GPro99-33) Rich Leadbetter of _[Sega Saturn Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Saturn_Magazine "Sega Saturn Magazine")_ said it "is far more of a gratifying experience to the average gamer than [VF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtua_Fighter_/(video_game/) "Virtua Fighter (video game)") or its sequel"[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-SatMag12-29) and a _Next Generation_ reviewer concluded, "_VF2_ is one of the best games of all time, but _Fighting Vipers_ nearly eclipses it."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-NGen24-28) In Japan, _[Famitsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famitsu "Famitsu")_ scored it 37 out of 40.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-fam-30)

### Sequels and re-releases

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fighting_Vipers&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Sequels and re-releases")\]

A [sequel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequel "Sequel"), _[Fighting Vipers 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers_2 "Fighting Vipers 2")_ was released, introducing new characters. It was ported to the [Dreamcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreamcast "Dreamcast") but only in Japan and Europe.

All of the _Fighting Vipers_ characters were used in Sega AM2's _[Fighters Megamix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighters_Megamix "Fighters Megamix")_ for the Sega Saturn. _Fighting Vipers_ was also re-released for the [PlayStation 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_2 "PlayStation 2") as part of the [Sega Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Ages "Sega Ages") line. A PAL version was planned, but never released.

_Fighting Vipers_ was re-released in late 2012 on PlayStation Network and Xbox Live as one of five games included in the Sega Model 2 Collection. The re-release features online play, but does not contain any of the extra content found in the Saturn version. _Fighting Vipers_ is also included as a playable arcade game in _[Judgment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judgment_/(video_game/) "Judgment (video game)")_ and _[Lost Judgment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_Judgment "Lost Judgment")_.

Bahn appears as a solo unit in _[Project X Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_X_Zone "Project X Zone")_, a Nintendo 3DS RPG crossover of [Capcom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capcom "Capcom"), Sega and [Namco Bandai Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namco_Bandai_Games "Namco Bandai Games").

A programmer working on _Fighting Vipers_ put [Sonic the Hedgehog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_the_Hedgehog_/(character/) "Sonic the Hedgehog (character)") and [Tails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_%22Tails%22_Prower "Miles \"Tails\" Prower") in the game for amusement, which led to Sega AM2 commissioning a _Sonic_ fighting game, _Sonic the Fighters_.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-34) Hidden within the data of the arcade version of _Sonic the Fighters_ is an additional character named Honey,[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Vipers#cite_note-35) a yellow cat wearing Candy's red plastic fairy costume. She is only playable by hacking the game's data. Honey's model was removed from the _Sonic the Fighters_ port on _[Sonic Gems Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_Gems_Collection "Sonic Gems Collection")_. However, in the [Xbox 360](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_360 "Xbox 360") and [PlayStation 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_3 "PlayStation 3") port, she is a playable character, and was later introduced to the cast of [Archie Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Comics "Archie Comics")' _[Sonic the Hedgehog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_the_Hedgehog_/(comics/) "Sonic the Hedgehog (comics)")_ comics during an arc based on _Sonic the Fighters_. The arc depicts Honey as a fashion designer similar to her human counterpart, and also features a [boar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boar "Boar") character based on Jane.

14.content:
It’s been roughly a year since the Combing Through the Pages feature was started, and we’ve finally reached this point: despite saying multiple times Tips & Tricks is my favorite video gaming magazine ever, it has yet to appear in this feature. In preparations to make the magazine’s debut on the site, I was holding out hope I still had a specific issue, and as fate would have it, November 1996 (Issue #21) remains in my possession.

![Image 1: TT21Banner](https://gemubaka.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/tt21banner.png?w=630)

My childhood magazine subscriptions were Nintendo Power and GamePro, but whenever I would visit extended family, my grandmother would take me to the local grocery store and let me pick out a magazine each time. This saw me picking up a couple of issues of VideoGames/Computer and VideoGames magazine. I vividly remember the April 1994 VideoGames issue for its behind-the-scenes look at Mortal Kombat II, which was my very first look behind the curtain at what went into digitizing the characters. In fact, whatever issue of VideoGames it was that featured the [NES game Captain Planet and Planeteers is what inspired the game’s entry on GemuBaka](https://gemubaka.com/2013/08/07/nes-review-captain-planet-and-the-planteers/).

This magazine eventually morphed into Tips & Tricks, and I guess I originally mistook the issues as being nothing more than a cheat book listing. While I have since recollected a couple of the earlier issues of the magazine, it was for some reason Issue #21 that I took a chance on the magazine and got completely hooked.

I’ve dropped the hint a couple of times this would be the next magazine feature ([the top third with the obscured view of June’s twintails](https://gemubaka.com/2023/12/25/bonus-combing-through-the-pages-the-midway-issue-no-1/) and [the feature image with this issue on top of stacked magazines](https://gemubaka.com/2023/11/28/a-shift-in-collecting-focus-publications/)). So, without further ado, let’s get to Tips & Tricks!

* * *

#### ABOUT COMBING THROUGH THE PAGES

Since I really like video games, it should come as no surprise that I also really like video gaming magazines. At times I leaf through issues of magazines such as Tips & Tricks, Electronic Gaming Monthly and Nintendo Power, and I would share bits and pieces of that content through tweets. After a handful of issues, I figured I should really just collect these thoughts and make proper features out of them for GemuBaka.

To preface this and get it out of the way – if you came here expecting to find a PDF or similar file that provides a perfectly-scanned collection of every single page of this magazine … I’m afraid you won’t find that here. The intent of this feature is to break down the magazine featured and then roll in my personal thoughts and experiences on the subject matter, along with tying those points into features on GemuBaka when it is applicable. Today’s feature is Tips & Tricks Issue #21 (November 1996).

[The previous Combing Through the Pages entry was The Midway Issue No. 1.](https://gemubaka.com/2023/12/25/bonus-combing-through-the-pages-the-midway-issue-no-1/)

* * *

#### TIPS & TRICKS

Tips & Tricks was published by the Larry Flint Publishing company. This company certainly published … other magazines, but by my understanding, this came to pass through its acquisition of another publishing company. [Bill Kunkel worked for Tips & Tricks in his later years](https://gemubaka.com/?s=bill+kunkel&submit.x=0&submit.y=0), and he relayed to me some interesting stories about the shared workspace between the different magazines.

There was such a demand for cheat codes, tricks and strategies at the time, that the publisher could be convinced to evolve VideoGames into the Tips & Tricks format. While every other magazine at the time was multi-functioning and filled with game reviews and industry features, Tips & Tricks fully leaned into strategy guides and an encyclopedia-like cheat database in every issue.

The magazine would evolve to include a number of other genre- or game-specific features over time. It would also eventually feature a section of game previews, but this was mostly to judge interest from readers – the more they marked interest on the issue’s reader card, the more likely it was the game would eventually be featured with a strategy guide when it released.

Also, while other magazines would ebb and flow with arcade game coverage, Tips & Tricks was one of the publications that reliably stuck with the format until it was no longer viable. As I started being able to transport myself to the arcades in the mid-1990s, this was likely another reason Tips & Tricks really appealed to me. The magazine also wasn’t shy about sharing games and culture items from Japan, which also caught my attention.

The magazine started quarterly in 1994, moved to an issue every other month in 1995 and then went full monthly in 1996. This ran all the way through 150 issues and into the seventh generation of consoles. Tips & Tricks got to celebrate hitting 150 issues with its August 2007 publication, and then it was unceremoniously canned.

As disappointing as this was, it’s understandable given the original premise of the magazine. The internet had finally gotten its foot into the door of virtually every household at this point, and all interest then went into accessing free online cheat sites. In fact, I recall hearing Bill, and by extension Chris Bieniek, speak about the magazine having absolutely no online presence. That was something the staff tried to remedy, but it was likely a case of too little, too late.

The late aughts was really the final nail in the coffin for many established video game magazines, and very few have been made routinely available at the newsstand since that time.

But, when you actually picked up an issue of Tips & Tricks and read through its features, you could absolutely tell they were labors of love. I always saw the cheats section as a “bonus” you got with the magazine, especially as it grew over time with more features and touched on worldwide gaming culture. Especially with reviews, other magazines seemed to be trying to convince or persuade you, but reading Tips & Tricks seemed more like a publication giving you information to make the most out of the games on which you were spending money.

I saw the possibility of working for Tips & Tricks to be a dream job, but it wasn’t in the cards for me as I didn’t finish college until a few years after the magazine ceased publication. It technically continued on after 2007 with occasional cheat book publications, but these certainly did not contain the same spirit as the impressive run of the magazine.

[There is an archived feature originally published on Game Losers detailing an oral history of the magazine](https://web.archive.org/web/20140825013348/http://gamelosers.net/blog/2014/07/23/tips-tricks/), so if you want a deep dive into Tips & Tricks, I recommend giving that a read.

* * *

#### THE MAGAZINE COVER

![Image 2: IMG_8943](https://gemubaka.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/img_8943.jpg?w=526&h=704)

_(This is my personal copy of the 1996 magazine I had to hide so my parents wouldn’t throw it away, so, yes, I’m fully aware it’s a little beat up)_

The cover of Tips & Tricks Issue #21 fits in the publication’s formula, but that’s a good thing as there is plenty to catch your eye at the newsstand.

The top third is reserved for the color strip and blocky, noticeable title “TIPS & TRICKS,” and, of course, this is “THE #1 VIDEO-GAME TIPS MAGAZINE.” The magazine started using this top third with its July 1995 issue, one issue after it started its bimonthly circulation. Tips & Tricks used this color strip monthly from issues 6-27 until it started to drop the color strip and overlay the Tips & Tricks logo into the cover’s game art background.

One thing I never noticed until I start typing out this feature: From issues 1-20, the VideoGames magazine branding was worked into this top third as vertical text next to the magazine’s logo. Issue #21 drops this and replaces it with a format listing. This specific issue includes arcade, Super NES, PlayStation, Genesis, Saturn, Nintendo 64, 3D0 and portable system content.

The featured game for this issue is Capcom’s Star Gladiator. Front and center is a promotional art for the game featuring the character June. The game logo is also prominently displayed, noting this game comes “from the makers of Street Fighter.” Fighting games were still pretty hot at this time, so there was a lot of attention toward Capcom slowly moving into the field of 3D fighting games. This is likely what caught my attention on the newsstand for this issue, as I can’t recall any other U.S. magazine putting Star Gladiator on its cover.

Then, along the right side, there are a number of capsules placed to catch your attention based on all manner of different games. Super Mario 64, having just been released in 1996, continued to get magazine coverage. This is joined by a number of arcade-based capsules featuring Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo, Ninja Master’s, Fighting Vipers and Galaxy Fight. What a lineup of games. And all of this is joined by some sort of Pepsiman guy.

It’s like this cover was designed for 15-year-old me. It hits all of the niche interests I’m into, but in that moment of time, this was what was actually popular. Arcades were still popping, and fighting games served as the genre of the moment. Doubly so, this was still a time when people anticipated hit arcade games would eventually receive console versions, so the arcade sector of the industry was closely followed by a lot of people.

More people were finding themselves owning systems such as the PlayStation and Saturn, and the Nintendo 64 had become the shiny new toy. This was the point the fifth generation of consoles was going to start snowballing into the popularity it eventually earned as the fourth generation started cooling off.

The cover also signifies there may be codes and cheats inside this magazine.

* * *

#### THE CONTENTS

![Image 3: IMG_8946](https://gemubaka.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/img_8946.jpg?w=454&h=604)

Being one of the earlier issues of Tips & Tricks, Issue #21 is essentially split into two parts: the strategy guides and the codes. Strategy guides for this issue include Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo, Ninja Master’s, Star Gladiator and Super Mario 64 (part two). There are approximately 25 pages of codes and tips in this issue, with sections dedicated to the Super Nintendo, Genesis, PlayStation, Saturn, Game Boy, Game Gear, 3D0 and arcade, along with a page of Game Genie/Game Shark codes.

In between these, there are a few sections such as an introduction page, reader mail, an XBand leaderboard listing and a section featuring executive editor Betty Hallock.

The introduction page, named “Power Up!” in the magazine, features a spread of the staff with a note from Betty Hallock. She states she is moving to New York and will no longer work at the magazine, but she is still willing to contribute.

Chris Bieniek is the editor in chief, Ione Flores is art director and Nicholas Constant is listed as senior editor/contributing art director, among other credits listed for the Tips & Tricks staff.

The reader mail section is fairly straightforward in this issue. A reader notes having trouble finding the magazine on newsstands, and another laments the loss of having an issue stolen from them at school. A question is asked about having an Ultra 64/Nintendo 64 code section (this would start in the December 1996 issue) and another asks about an arcade code section (started in this very issue).

Tips & Tricks is asked by one reader about Wing Commander IV releasing on the 3D0, but this would unfortunately not happen. There is a letter sent to Betty about the Japanese super hero Parman mentioned in a previous issue, and another letter to Betty is a person being pretty weird. Yeah, this definitely fit into the time period where guys got extremely weird about finding out that women played video games as well.

The reader mail section also featured a capsule I always enjoyed: The Token of the Month. Readers could send the magazine an arcade token, and Tips & Tricks would feature one per month and it would serve as the “console icon” for any arcade sections featured in that issue. The Issue #21 token was from Bullwinkle’s in Santa Clara, California.

Also in this section was a run of short four-panel comics, and this issue’s comic features … Johnny Turbo? Huh.

* * *

#### STRATEGY GUIDES

**Fighting Vipers**  
In a follow-up to strategies printed for the arcade game Fighting Vipers, there is a one-page feature on Candy’s/Honey’s armor break when your character has 100 or more wins in versus mode. Normally, a lower armor break on the character shatters Candy’s leg armor, but at 100 or more wins, a break also smashes Candy’s skirt.

A number of notes are made on this process, as it is obviously kind of tedious. The magazine notes your armor guage will change its pose every eight victories, and there were time attacks to see how fast a round could be won. Tips & Tricks notes if you can win a round in nine seconds or less, you are a top-notch player.

Tips & Tricks took a variety of screenshots on an arcade cabinet and made sure to note if you were to try this in an arcade, it would cost you a lot of money – 50 cents per play would add up to $50 for 100 wins if you allowed one player to continually win. Tips & Tricks also touches on the eventual Saturn release of the game, noting it was unknown at the time if this would work in the home release.

![Image 4: IMG_8949](https://gemubaka.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/img_8949.jpg?w=456&h=649)

**Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo**  
[I touched on this in my GemuBaka feature on Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo](https://gemubaka.com/2023/04/09/my-favorite-easter-video-game-super-puzzle-fighter-ii-turbo/), but magazine coverage like this is what drew me into eventually picking up this game on PlayStation. Tips & Tricks at this time covered the arcade version of the game, as I mentioned in my feature that I am very unclear as to whether the console version released in 1996 or 1997.

This strategy guide breaks down all of the basics of the game, noting Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo is kind of like a cross between Puyo Puyo and [Tetris (Battle) Gaiden](https://gemubaka.com/2021/05/20/retro-achiever-game-57-tetris-battle-gaiden/). Those are things that didn’t mean anything to me in 1996, but they get a nod of approval from me in 2024.

This feature shows a lot of the really cool artwork from the game, and it shows some of the neat hidden features of the game – most notably in accessing the three hidden characters Akuma, Dan and Devilot. If you want to dig deeper, there are short breakdowns of each character showing off their counter gem patterns. The guide does a great job of pointing out that constantly going for huge counter drops is not always the best approach, and mixing up large and small attacks can be a better strategy.

**Ninja Master’s**  
I still have yet to see this game in an arcade. If it weren’t for this issue of Tips & Tricks, I’d probably have no idea this game existed. It does get played at times at game centers such as Mikado, but it always sticks out to me as a fighting game I should check out and then I just never get around to it.

And, yes, the apostrophe is part of the game title.

This guide offers up a setup of the basics and then codes for a time attack mode and a boss code to play as Ranmaru and Nobunaga. Then, as expected, you get a section detailing all of the characters’ special moves.

**Star Gladiator**  
The cover feature of the issue, Tips & Tricks breaks down the basics of Star Gladiator Episode I: Final Crusade. It was noted the game was available at the time in arcades, and the PlayStation version would be available in November 1996. Despite this, this guide is labeled as a PlayStation feature.

As a Capcom game entering the third dimension, there is a section that details a number of elements such as dodging, air attacks, juggles, ring outs and special finishes, wake-up movement and energy blocks.

Most of the guide is a character breakdown with special attack inputs, but Star Gladiator has a mechanic that involves string attack charts. Each character has a predetermined chart of attacks that flow together into attack strings. Each character has their chart printed out in this guide, and it concludes with a chart that lists every base input (direction + button) and marking each character that has a move corresponding to that input.

![Image 5: IMG_8950](https://gemubaka.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/img_8950.jpg?w=532&h=361)

**Super Mario 64**  
This is another magazine issue with big coverage on Super Mario 64, and this is part two of three for strategies in Tips & Tricks. This is essentially the stretch of the game following the first Bowser fight, going into the second.

Obviously, Super Mario 64 has a number of stars hidden in each course, and most guides detail how to retrieve each star along with screenshots.

* * *

#### CODES

I’m obviously not going to type out the pages and pages of codes and tips here, but it was common for Tips & Tricks to also print mini-features along the bottom of these pages.

![Image 6: IMG_8955](https://gemubaka.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/img_8955.jpg?w=630)

In this issue, the SEGA Saturn tip section features my very first exposure to the Pepsiman character. Pepsiman is featured as a hidden fighter in the Japanese versions of Fighting Vipers. Tips & Tricks actually explains who Pepsiman is, featuring screencaps from a Japanese Pepsi commercial where Pepsiman rushes to the aid of a screaming child. It is also pointed out there is a Pepsiman audio mini-CD, which is where the theme song’s “techno” and “jungle” mixes originate.

Pepsiman is far more known these days, but this served as an interesting footnote for the time that made reading Tips & Tricks more enjoyable for me.

Not much else sticks out in the codes section in this issue, though. For me, I do think it is interesting to see the code sections for the PlayStation and Saturn roughly one year into each console’s life. The PlayStation is highlighted with codes for games such as 3D Lemmings, Alien Trilogy, Battle Arena Toshinden, Jumping Flash!, Ridge Racer and Tekken; and the Saturn is highlighted with games such as Baku Baku Animal, Bug!, Clockwork Knight, Guardian Heroes and Panzer Dragoon.

The portable system and 3D0 sections are three strips that share the same page, but there are Game Boy codes for Killer Instinct and Wario Land and Game Gear codes for Ax Battler and Sonic Chaos. The games chosen to represent the 3D0 this month: Battlesport, Captain Quazar, Doom, Foes of Ali, Johnny Bazookatone and Rebel Assault.

As noted earlier, the arcade section debuted in this issue. This largely stems from secret characters and modes hidden in fighting games, as well as the wealth of secrets in games such as NBA Jam. There are some added secrets for games such as Area 51, Cruisin’ USA, Daytona USA and Killer Instinct 2. This section also features a lower strip, with the magazine showing readers that options menus do exist in arcade games (beyond the days when they were toggled with on-board dip switches). This particular feature looks at the test menu of Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo.

Lastly, there is one page dedicated to Game Genie/Game Shark codes. These include Aaahh!! Real Monsters on SEGA Genesis, Killer Instinct on Game Boy, Earthworm Jim on Game Gear; and then Tekken 2, Tokyo Highway Battle, NFL Quarterback Club ’97, Bogey Dead 6 and Star Fighter on PlayStation; and Alien Trilogy, Impact Racing, Star Fighter, Virtua Fighter Kids and World Series Baseball 2 on Saturn.

For the time, these were super handy sections to have on hand for games like NBA Jam or fighting games, and they ensured you would pick up the magazine again beyond reading it for the first time.

* * *

#### OTHER FEATURES

Pages remaining for this issue are the XBand Top 5 Lists and Betty’s Index.

![Image 7: IMG_4491](https://gemubaka.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/img_4491.jpg?w=531&h=398)

I’ve poked fun at the sealed XBand modem I’ve seen at a couple of swap meets, but this was a pretty cool gadget for its time. It allowed for select games to be played via modem on the Super Nintendo and SEGA Genesis.

For the month ending Sept. 1, 1996, here is who Tips & Tricks printed as the top 5 players in select games:

SEGA Genesis – Super Street Fighter II  
1\. -(O.G.187)-; 2. – (Pyrate69) -; 3. THE GAME DEMON; 4. MAVERICK18; 5. -(Nothingness)-  
SEGA Genesis – Mortal Kombat II  
1\. Mid-Knight Lover; 2. SHAMGOD!!!; 3. The Master Jon; 4. Kosd1R-?-Bandit!; 5. NECRON  
SEGA Genesis – Mortal Kombat 3  
1\. Starlite; 2. THE UNKNOWN XXX; 3. Koma; 4. WARLOCK!!!; 5. The Master Jon  
Super Nintendo – Super Street Fighter II  
1\. Dream Theater+; 2. Mr. Win Collector; 3. Phat Lady -TGF-; 4. ViRuS (U\*D); 5. Gorby’s Birthmark  
Super Nintendo – Mortal Kombat II  
1\. Jack LOVES Brie!; SiZZAHANDZ P.i.; 3. WaR GodD; 4. RIDGE RENEGADE; 5. NooB SaiboT-DEC-  
Super Nintendo – Killer Instinct  
1\. UnDeRtAkEr(TmB); 2. L ord G ame G od; 3. =Mr. Wizard=; 4. S e i f e r t; 5. DeStRo oF (U\*D)

![Image 8: IMG_8959](https://gemubaka.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/img_8959.jpg?w=457&h=609)

Betty’s Index would share a variety of gaming culture items, and this issue featured snippets of various candies. One of these is the Crunky bar – crunchy+chunky. I remember going out of my way to buy one of these the first time I saw it because of seeing it in this magazine.

This section also featured a variety of stickers from the Space Invaders franchise, a Pac-Man washcloth and Sonic the Hedgehog merch that included a pencil case, notepad and stickers.

* * *

#### ADVERTISING

This issue weighs in at 80 pages, so the advertising doesn’t hit as hard as something like Electronic Gaming Monthly, but there are definitely some interesting ads here.

As usual, I make note of the magazines’ self-advertising in the form of subscription notices. The first in this issue notes the magazine can be a holiday gift as December was on the horizon. A 12-issue, one-year subscription at this time was $19.95, but if you ordered multiple subscriptions as gifts, each additional subscription was $17.95. This saved “up to 70% off the annual cover price.” The cover price on this issue is $4.99.

![Image 9: IMG_8952](https://gemubaka.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/img_8952.jpg?w=461&h=655)

There is a second offer in this issue that caters to fans of Mortal Kombat that truly shows how off the charts this series was in the 1990s. For the holidays only, Tips & Tricks offered a special four-issue gift package for $19.95. This four-issue set included Issue #3 (Fall 1994 – Mortal Kombat II coverage for home consoles), Issue #11 (January 1996 – Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3 coverage), Issue #13 (March 1996 – Mortal Kombat 3 coverage) and Issue #14 (April 1996 – more Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3 coverage).

As a bonus, if you were among the first 300 to ordered the holiday gift package, Tips & Tricks would throw in a fifth issue, the “Mortal Kombat II Exposed” Issue #4 from Winter 1995 (the final quarterly issue). To sweeten the deal even more, if you opted to pay for a one-year subscription of the magazine at $19.95, this knocked the gift package price down to $10, so you would pay $29.95 for a one-year subscription and potentially five back issues.

It’s a shame $30 seemed like a ton of money to me back then … probably because, in my head, $30 was practically the price of a video game. That’s a deal I would jump on as an adult.

In other notes, at this time the Nintendo 64 had finally hit the public’s hands after a much-publicized delay. The inside front cover of the issue has a “Change the System” advertisement splashing all manner of information about the console across two pages.

The Nintendo 64 controller is billed as the most revolutionary video game interaction device ever, it has more than 50 titles in development covering all genres, expansion is planned to include more system RAM (and a readable-writable storage media that never happened) and a section tries to help you understand what items such as anti-aliasing, interpolation and texture mapping are supposed to mean. There is also an advertisement for a “Change the System” promotional VHS tape at a cost of $3.95.

![Image 10: IMG_8945](https://gemubaka.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/img_8945.jpg?w=485&h=324)

**Other advertisements**  
SEGA – Sonic 3D Blast for Genesis and Game Gear and Vectorman 2 on Genesis  
Bottom of the 9th – Konami – PlayStation and Saturn  
Samsung – Video game TV accessory with surround sound and multiple inputs  
Virtual Fighter – Saturn  
Street Racer – UbiSoft – PlayStation, Saturn and Game Boy  
Magic: The Gathering – Battlemage – Acclaim – PlayStation, Saturn, Windows 95  
Project Overkill – Konami – PlayStation  
Hexen – GT Interactive – PlayStation, Saturn, Windows 95, Macintosh (hey, this is a first for me in getting to mention the Mac format!)  
WipeOut XL – Psygnosis – PlayStation  
Arcadium – A social website based on gaming  
Advanced Dungeons & Dragons Iron & Blood Warriors of Ravenloft – Acclaim – PlayStation, Saturn, DOS CD-ROM (this ultimately only released on the PlayStation)  
NFL Quarterback Club ’97 – Acclaim – PlayStation, Saturn, DOS CD-ROM  
Donkey Kong Land 2/Game Boy Pocket – Nintendo  
Impact Racing – Acclaim – PlayStation, Saturn

It’s in these sections I also like to look at the mail order gaming stores that run advertisements. This issue has a Funco mail order form, presenting partial lists for NES, SNES, Genesis, PlayStation, Game Boy, Saturn and Game Gear. An NES system cost $25 at this point, with a great selection of games below $10. Plenty of games on the other formats were still holding some value at this time, as even the Super Nintendo and SEGA Genesis still had some fuel in the tank. You could also inquire about games for systems not listed, such as the SEGA CD and 3D0.

Game Quest also advertised, but it bucks the trend by not detailing any game offerings or pricing. However, it notes the store is running a buy one, get one half off deal, and cartridge games were buy two, get one free. Its big marketing for the month was a contest that offered a free video game console, which could include the brand-new Nintendo 64! In a nod of approval to this ad, it does dare to mention products in stock include formats such as the Jaguar CD and Virtual Boy.

![Image 11: IMG_8957](https://gemubaka.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/img_8957.jpg?w=451&h=625)

* * *

After a lot of talk, it feels great to get Tips & Tricks included in the magazine mix on GemuBaka. This was a really nostalgic read for me, and you can bet this magazine will return to Combing Through the Pages.

After cataloging my magazines, I noticed two specific magazines for which I only seem to have one, single issue. I’m debating where to head next, but the next Combing Through the Pages feature might take a bit of a detour from the typical video gaming magazine …

==========================
Fighting Vipers -- Notice --

Common Arts and Notice

f - forward, b - back, u - up, d - down, g - guard, p - punch, k - kick
   (upper case - hold lever/button)

 + : press the buttons simutaneously

And we use the following codes:
 (Crouch) : when you are crouchting (lever is neutral)
 (Back) : facing to the enemy's back
 (Dash) : dashing on
 (Air) : in the air
 (Wall) : near the wall

Command List
These commands may not be accurate. Art names with () is not
deterministic.
Art names may be changed that of before.
Inputs not defined the commands may not work well (like P+K).
In Notice column, we omitted the character's full name.(GBRTSJHP)
In Hit column, H means Hi-Attack(Standing Guard or Crouching is defensable),
M is Middle-Attack(Standing Guard is defensable), and L is Low-Attack
(Crouchng Guard is defensable or Small Jump is avoidable).

*Armor Breaker*
  Armor Breaker arts can destroy enemy's armor
when the armor gage is flashing.
They can also negate the effect of enemy's Guard Attack.
The arts below basically make the enemy down.

(Breast Armor Breaker) f f P  H only GRSJH

 *Guard & Attack*
  Guard & Attack arts can guard enemy's Hi or Middle Attack
and make counter attack. They also destroy enemy's armor.
You may be thrown untill the hit-judgement occurs.

(Guard & Punch)  b P  M only GBRJHP
(Guard & Kick)  b K  M only GRTSHP

 *Dashing Attack*
  These arts are available when you are dashing.
They also destroy enemy's armor.

(Dashing Straight) (Dash)P  M
(Shoulder Tackle) (Dash)P+G M
(Dashing Kick etc.) (Dash)K  M
(Slinding Kick)  (Dash)d or d/f K L

 *Throw*
  You can throw enemy close in fighting.
If you failed, the character grabs nothing,
and you may be thrown by enemy. 
There are some arts only if you faces to the wall.

Wall Throw  P+G  Throw
(Wall Press)  (Wall)P+G Throw
(Auto Wall Press) (Wall)PPP HHThrow except B

 *Down Attack*
  These are available when enemy is down.
If you failed, the character can't move for a while,
and you may be thrown by enemy.

(Stepping on)  u P  Down
(Soccer Ball Kick) d K  Down
(Punching Down)  d P  Down  only BRJHP

“ソニック”シリーズのキャラクターによる3D対戦格闘、『ソニック・ザ・ファイターズ』プレイインプレッション_01](https://www.famitsu.com/images/000/025/406/l_50becd1959a70.jpg)](https://www.famitsu.com/images/000/025/406/l_50becd1959a70.jpg) 『[**ソニック・ザ・ファイターズ**](https://www.famitsu.com/search/?q=%E3%82%BD%E3%83%8B%E3%83%83%E3%82%AF%E3%83%BB%E3%82%B6%E3%83%BB%E3%83%95%E3%82%A1%E3%82%A4%E3%82%BF%E3%83%BC%E3%82%BA&type=game-title)』は、1996年5月にアーケードでリリースされたタイトルで、“ソニック”シリーズの21年という長い歴史の中でも唯一の3D対戦格闘ゲームだ。当時セガサターンへの移植が予定されていたが、残念ながら実現しなかった本作が、“MODEL 2 COLLECTION”の作品のひとつとして、プレイステーションネットワークとXbox LIVE アーケードで配信された。 　1996年というと、対戦格闘ゲームブーム後半、よく言えば群雄割拠、ぶっちゃけていうと玉石混合な時代だった記憶がある。とはいえ、各社から毎月のように新作タイトルがリリースされていて、ゲームセンターに非常に活気のあった時代だ。3D格闘ゲームは、『[**バーチャファイター2（ver.2.1）**](https://www.famitsu.com/search/?q=%E3%83%90%E3%83%BC%E3%83%81%E3%83%A3%E3%83%95%E3%82%A1%E3%82%A4%E3%82%BF%E3%83%BC2%EF%BC%88ver.2.1%EF%BC%89)』の人気が圧倒的で、それに対抗すべく各社からさまざまな3D格闘が投入されていた。ナムコ（現バンダイナムコゲームズ）の『[**鉄拳**](https://www.famitsu.com/search/?q=%E9%89%84%E6%8B%B3&type=game-title)』シリーズのように、いまでは3D格闘を代表するにまでなったタイトルから、『[**スターグラディエイター**](https://www.famitsu.com/search/?q=%E3%82%B9%E3%82%BF%E3%83%BC%E3%82%B0%E3%83%A9%E3%83%87%E3%82%A3%E3%82%A8%E3%82%A4%E3%82%BF%E3%83%BC&type=game-title)』（カプコン）、『[**闘神伝**](https://www.famitsu.com/search/?q=%E9%97%98%E7%A5%9E%E4%BC%9D&type=game-title)』（アーケード版『2』はカプコンからリリース、開発はタムソフト）のように、残念ながら格ゲーブームの衰退とともに表舞台から姿を消したタイトルも。当時は、いまのようにインターネットも発達しておらず、娯楽があふれ返っているという状況でもなかったので、大量の格闘ゲームが登場しても、それぞれにそれなりに時間を割いて楽しむことができていた、ゲームにとってはけっこういい時代。 　そんな中リリースされた『ソニック・ザ・ファイターズ』だが、当時は『[**VF2**](https://www.famitsu.com/search/?q=VF2&type=game-title)』のリリースから2年経ち、『3』への期待が高まっていたということもあり、残念ながらそれほど話題には上らなかった。そのためか筆者の通っていたゲームセンターでは、わりとすぐに姿を消してしまったので、ほとんど対戦することができなかったことを記憶している。今回はオンライン対戦に対応しているので、16年の時を経て、ついに気軽に対戦することができるようになった。 広告 初心者向けのシンプルな3D対戦格闘ゲーム -------------------- 本作は『[**VF**](https://www.famitsu.com/search/?q=VF&type=game-title)』シリーズを開発しているAM2研が制作していることもあり、基本的なシステムは『VF』を、判定や動きの雰囲気は本作の前年にリリースされた『[**ファイティングバイパーズ**](https://www.famitsu.com/search/?q=%E3%83%95%E3%82%A1%E3%82%A4%E3%83%86%E3%82%A3%E3%83%B3%E3%82%B0%E3%83%90%E3%82%A4%E3%83%91%E3%83%BC%E3%82%BA&type=game-title)』を踏襲しているといっていい。パンチ（P）、キック（K）の攻撃ボタンとガードに相当するバリア（B）ボタンの3ボタンで対戦を行い、それぞれの入力順や組み合わせでコンボや技が発生する、いまとなってはおなじみのシステムだ。 　攻撃を出すとキャラの手足が大きくなったり、ダメージを受けてダウンするとぺちゃんこになってソニックシリーズのダメージ表現でおなじみのリングが飛び散るなど、ディフォルメされた演出が随所に見られ、リアルに重きを置いていた当時の3D対戦格闘と比べると派手な見た目となっている。また、3D格闘で一般的な上・中・下段の読み合いが必要なく、シンプルな対戦が行える。基本は打撃とバリア、投げの3すくみで、そこにP＋K＋B同時押しで出せる回避が絡んでくる。ある意味『[**VF3**](https://www.famitsu.com/search/?q=VF3&type=game-title)』に先駆けて三次元的な移動が全キャラで可能になったタイトルとも言えるかもしれない。ちなみに回避は、相手の近くで攻撃に合わせて出すと演出付きで後ろに回り込んでくれるのだが、そのあと逆に反撃を受けてしまったりして、筆者の腕ではうまくコンボに組み込んだりすることはできなかった。ファングの銃やビーンの爆弾を回避しつつ反撃するのには重要な行動だし、多分キャラごとに確定反撃技などを見つければいいのだろうが、そこはいまさらながらやりこみ勢に期待したい。このようにそれほど複雑なシステムではないことに加え、ボタンを適当に連打するだけでも状況に応じてコンボを出してくれる“オートマチック”モードも用意されているので、まさに“3D格闘初心者向け”を意識して作られたタイトルだといえるだろう。 ▲コミカルな演出で、適当にガチャガチャ操作しているだけでも見た目に楽しい。3D格闘としての基礎はしっかりしているので、回避などを駆使してちゃんと闘っても十分に遊べる。 本作で特徴的な点にバリアの存在が挙げられる。それぞれのキャラクターは対戦開始時に5つのバリアを持っていて、特定の攻撃をガードすると破壊され、すべてなくなると攻撃を一切ガードできなくなってしまう。バリアを破壊できる攻撃は、総じて隙が大きいので反撃は比較的容易なのだが、バリアの残り数はラウンド持ち越しなので、後半ラウンドで逆転されることも。また、一定時間技の硬直が短くなる“ハイパーモード”を発動するのにもバリアを1個消費するので、ラウンドごとではなく3本先取の全体の流れを考えながら闘う必要があるのだ。上・中・下段を廃していることに対するフォローの意味合いもあるのだと思うが、このシステムがスパイスとなっていて、意外と（失礼！）幅広いレベルのプレイヤーが楽しめるのではないだろうか。 白の時空**](https://www.famitsu.com/search/?q=%E3%82%BD%E3%83%8B%E3%83%83%E3%82%AF%E3%82%B8%E3%82%A7%E3%83%8D%E3%83%AC%E3%83%BC%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A7%E3%83%B3%E3%82%BA+%E7%99%BD%E3%81%AE%E6%99%82%E7%A9%BA&type=game-title)』（PS3／Xbox 360）など、さまざまなタイトルで見ることができる。　ビーンとバークは、『ソニック』シリーズでは本作にしか登場していないオリジナルキャラで、アメコミ版“ソニック”にはたびたび出演している、ある意味レアなキャラクターだ（ちなみにビーンは、1988年にアーケードでリリースされた横スクロールアクション『[**ダイナマイトダックス**](https://www.famitsu.com/search/?q=%E3%83%80%E3%82%A4%E3%83%8A%E3%83%9E%E3%82%A4%E3%83%88%E3%83%80%E3%83%83%E3%82%AF%E3%82%B9)』のキャラクターが元になっていたりする）。全キャラを詳しく知っている人は相当の“ソニック”マニアではないだろうか。 　またメインの8人に加えて、PSN／XBLA版ではアーケード版にはなかった隠しキャラ“ハニー・ザ・キャット”がいる。“ハニー・ザ・キャット”はアーケード版のデータ内に存在していたボツキャラクター。その存在自体はファンのあいだでは知られていたものの、実際にプレイすることはできなかったので、今回PSN／XBLA版で初めて日の目を見ることとなった。その見た目からわかるように、『ファイティングバイパーズ』の“ハニー”がベースになっている。同じく隠しキャラとしてボスのメタルソニックとDr.エッグマンも使用可能だが、3キャラともランクマッチでは使用することができないのが残念なところだ（プレイヤーマッチやオフライン対戦では使用可能）。とくにメタルソニックとDr.エッグマンは敵として登場するそのままの性能で、ちょっと強すぎるため当然かもしれないが、性能を調整するなどしてランクマッチでも使用できるとうれしかったところだ。 ▲アーケード版で使用できなかったキャラで遂にプレイ可能！　ハニー、メタルソニック、エッグマンは、それぞれ、エミー、ソニック、ビーンにカーソルを合わせてスタートボタンを押すことで選択可能だ。 懐かしさを噛みしめながらプレイするべし ------------------- 『VF』、『鉄拳』によって3D格闘が脚光を浴びてはいたものの、それまでスタンダードだった2D格闘の考えかたが通用しないこともあり、二の足を踏んでいたプレイヤーがいたことは事実。そういう人たちにも門戸を開くという意味では、『ソニック・ザ・ファイターズ』と本作の直前にリリースされた『[**バーチャファイター キッズ**](https://www.famitsu.com/search/?q=%E3%83%90%E3%83%BC%E3%83%81%E3%83%A3%E3%83%95%E3%82%A1%E3%82%A4%E3%82%BF%E3%83%BC+%E3%82%AD%E3%83%83%E3%82%BA&type=game-title)』がかなりがんばっていたのではないかと、久しぶりにプレイしていると当時のことがぼんやりと思い起こされてきた。そういう意味では、1996年当時ゲーセンでプレイしていた人や、気になっていたけど近所のゲーセンに入荷せずに遊べなかった人などにおすすめ。本作そのものの思い出だけでなく、当時のことを思い起こすトリガーとして利用してみるのはいかがだろうか。 　なにぶん古いうえ、正直対戦格闘ゲームとしてはマイナーな部類に入るので、オンラインでの対戦相手はそれほど多くはない。しかし、MODEL 2 COLLECTIONの移植チームが中心となって、対戦イベントなどの開催を考えているそうなので、年末に向けて盛り上がりに期待したい。 　なお実績／トロフィーはオフラインのみで達成可能で、達成難度も低い。同時にリリースされた『VF2』や『ファイティングバイパーズ』と比べても、CPUの難易度が低めなぶん、3D格ゲーに慣れていない人でもすぐに解除できるだろう。実績／トロフィーマニアの方にもオススメの逸品だ。 ■著者紹介：黒鉄タカスエ
